title: AES-128 Eight late faults: full-key recovery (Piret–Quisquater 2003)

target.description: Full ten-round AES-128. Two useful late faults for each of four last-round-key groups (eight total) provide candidate material for the complete final-round key; the master key follows by AES-128 key-schedule inversion and candidate verification.

setting.key_relation: One unchanged secret AES-128 master key; no related-key or key-schedule-fault oracle.
setting.key_population: AES-128 keys in the stated unprotected single-byte-fault model; no weak-key restriction.
setting.plaintext_model: A correct ciphertext and its faulty counterpart for each plaintext; different pairs may use different plaintexts. The source's algorithm associates every pair with the same key.

fault_model.target: A byte of the AES encryption state; faults in the key schedule are outside this result.
fault_model.granularity: One initial byte with an unknown nonzero difference; later diffusion may change four or sixteen state bytes.
fault_model.timing: After the round-8 diffusion layer and before the round-9 diffusion layer (theta_(R−2) to theta_(R−1)); the source's theta is ShiftRows followed by MixColumns.
fault_model.location: Acquire two useful faults in each of the four position classes that cover disjoint four-byte final-round-key groups. The source calls these carefully chosen locations; arbitrary placement is not guaranteed to achieve coverage in eight attempts.
fault_model.value_control: The faulty byte value is random and assumed uniformly distributed; no chosen difference or bit-level fault control.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty ciphertext has its correct counterpart for the same plaintext and key; useful pairs are distinguished from total injection attempts.

assumptions: Only correct/faulty output pairs satisfying the stated single-byte model and timing window are counted.
The last-round-key candidate set is computed from differential constraints, and any remaining candidates require a separate check.
The paper instantiates and tests the 128-bit-block, 128-bit-key variant; its general extension remark is not a quantified AES-192/256 result.

In the source theta_r=ShiftRows_r followed by MixColumns_r. The four final-round-key groups in column-majorFIPSindices are{0,13,10,7}, {4,1,14,11}, {8,5,2,15}, {12,9,6,3}; these are affected sets, not ordered inverseMixColumns arguments.

time.note: No numeric end-to-end runtime is stated for this specific endpoint. Candidate-list sizes and candidate-search space are not substituted for time.

data.note: Section 3.3 counts eight carefully placed useful faults: two for each four-byte group. Each requires its correct ciphertext counterpart. This is not eight arbitrary injection attempts.

memory.note: Section 2 stores differential patterns D and candidate lists L but does not tabulate whole-attack peak memory.

preprocessing.note: Section 2 forms a table of 255*n single-byte-fault diffusion patterns. For one AES column n=4, this gives 1020 patterns as a derived component count, not a reported total preprocessing-time budget.

success.description: Plug-in conservative full-key estimate at eight useful late-fault pairs: two pairs for each of four disjoint final-round-key groups. Adopt the reported rounded98% local singleton frequency as the applicable marginal model for every group. If each population marginal is at least0.98, the union bound gives complete-key success at least0.92 without group independence. All four singleton lists yield the unique true last-round key, and AES128 schedule inversion yields the original master key using the existing data. Because98% is an empirical frequency without a trial denominator, rounding rule or uncertainty bound, the displayed approximately92% is an empirical-marginal-model estimate, not a measured whole-key rate, an unconditional AES guarantee or a statistical confidence lower bound. Transfer of the local observation to each of the four group marginals is a modeling condition, not four measured marginal bounds. No0.98^4 independence product is used. The77% experiment and few-second runtime concern the separate two-earlier-fault attack; they are not transferred. Physical acquisition, timing and two-per-group coverage are conditioned upon, not priced or assigned a yield.

review.scope: Read all12 exact-edition pages including AppendixA. Reconstructed the sufficient joint singleton event, source98% local measurement, conditional four-marginal union envelope and deterministic AES128 key-schedule inversion. Statistical uncertainty, group transfer and acquisition conditions retained. Both original local components, all native resources and the independent two-earlier-fault endpoint remain unchanged. Targeted success review, not a new full-paper/forward audit.

components.description: Sections2/3.3: at correctly modeled effective late-byte faults, the actual last-round-key bytes satisfy each column equation and survive intersections. Retention alone does not prove four groups are simultaneously unique.

Section3.3 reports98% unique identification of ONE four-byte final-subkey group from two useful late-fault pairs, without a trial denominator. This is not the whole-key success for eight useful faults.

evidence.locator: CHES2003 PDF2–5/printed78–81 Section2; PDF8/printed84 Section3.3 four-group/eight-late-fault construction and local98% observation; PDF11–12/printed87–88 AppendixA. Targeted success review2026-11-07.
evidence.interpretation: Supersedes only the earlier absence of a composed primary model estimate. For four singleton events U_j, union gives Pr(all U_j)>=1-sum_j(1-p_j); substituting the reported rounded local0.98 as each adopted marginal gives the approximately0.92 empirical-model lower envelope. No group independence, directly measured full-key frequency, confidence interval or actual-population marginal lower bound is asserted. The true key is uniquely assembled on this sufficient event, so this is a complete-output estimate rather than promoting local retention alone.

limitations: Useful correct/faulty pairs exclude acquisition failures and faults outside the model; total physical attempts are not costed.
Computer experiments in this paper do not establish a measured physical fault-injection setup.
